reps.prompt:
Historical Context: Prohibition. Throughout United States history, many constitutional and civic issues have been debated by Americans. These debates have resulted in efforts by individuals, groups, and governments to address these issues. These efforts have achieved varying degrees of success. One of these constitutional and civic issues is Prohibition.

Task: Using information from the documents and your knowledge of United States history, write an essay in which you
• Describe the historical circumstances surrounding this constitutional or civic issue
• Explain efforts by individuals, groups, and/or governments to address this constitutional or civic issue
• Discuss the impact of the efforts on the United States and/or on American society

exam_meta.part: Part III B — Civic Literacy Essay

stimulus.content: . . . The prohibition movement was an outgrowth of the temperance crusades of the first half of the nineteenth century. Hard drinking was almost the rule among the Fathers of the Republic. The per capita consumption of spirits in the early days was many times what it is now, and beer drinking was almost unknown. After the War of 1812, there grew up in the New England States a large commerce in West Indian rum, which was consumed extensively, especially in Maine, supplementing the consumption of heavy liquors which were manufactured in those States. Maine alone, in 1827, when her population was 360,000, manufactured 1,333,160 gallons of liquor, and it was sold at retail in nearly every store and tavern. Drunkenness in its worst form, involving disastrous social consequences, was widespread. Sufficient evidence of it was to be found in the number of persons in the jails and poorhouses. . . .
stimulus.image_alt: Text excerpt from L. Ames Brown’s article “Prohibition” in The North American Review, November 1915, tracing the movement’s roots in nineteenth-century temperance crusades.
stimulus.citation: Source: L. Ames Brown, “Prohibition,” The North American Review, November 1915
stimulus.provenance: NYSED Regents US History & Government, January 2026, Part III

stimulus.image_alt: 1919 Anti-Saloon League of America broadside titled “National Prohibition Ratification Map”: a United States map numbering the order in which states ratified the National Prohibition Amendment as of January 31, 1919, noting only four states had not yet ratified. Below, the Statement of the National Legislative Committee of the Anti-Saloon League calls ratification “the greatest victory for moral reform in America since the Declaration of Independence” and urges enforcement legislation from Congress and the states.
stimulus.provenance: NYSED Regents US History & Government, January 2026, Part III

reps.exemplar:
Prohibition was a constitutional and civic issue that tested how far government power should reach into the private behavior of citizens. The historical circumstances stretched back a century: as L. Ames Brown wrote in 1915, the prohibition movement was “an outgrowth of the temperance crusades of the first half of the nineteenth century,” when hard drinking was widespread and its consequences — poverty, crime, filled jails and poorhouses — were visible in every state. By the Progressive Era, reformers had turned a moral crusade into a constitutional campaign.

Individuals, groups, and governments all made efforts to address the issue. The Anti-Saloon League’s 1919 ratification map shows the campaign at its peak: forty-four states had ratified the Eighteenth Amendment by January 1919, and the League — which called ratification “the greatest victory for moral reform in America since the Declaration of Independence” — immediately pressed Congress for enforcement legislation, which came as the Volstead Act of 1919. For the first time, the federal government wrote a restriction on personal behavior into the Constitution itself.

The impact of these efforts fell far short of their aims. Enforcement proved nearly impossible: speakeasies multiplied in every city, organized crime figures like Al Capone built empires on bootlegging, and public respect for the rule of law eroded. By 1933 the country reversed itself, repealing Prohibition with the Twenty-first Amendment — the only amendment ever ratified to cancel another. Prohibition’s lasting impact was a civic lesson about the limits of constitutional power over private conduct: a reform without broad public consent cannot be enforced, no matter how noble its motive.
reps.compare_focus: Name the civic principle in play — here, the government’s constitutional power to regulate private behavior — and bring one piece of outside evidence the documents don’t hand you. The 3→4 move is outside information tied to the principle, not more document summary.
compare_checklist: Did I name the constitutional or civic principle at stake, in my own words?
Did I bring outside information — a law, amendment, court case, or event that is not in the documents?
Did I use evidence from both documents, cited by what they are?
Did I discuss impact — what changed — rather than only describing events?

reps.prompt:
Directions: Write a well-organized essay that includes an introduction, several paragraphs, and a conclusion. Use evidence from at least four documents in the body of the essay. Support your response with relevant facts, examples, and details. Include additional outside information.

Historical Context: Creation of a Stronger National Government
Throughout United States history, many constitutional and civic issues have been debated by Americans. These debates have resulted in efforts by individuals, groups, and governments to address these issues. These efforts have achieved varying degrees of success. One of these constitutional and civic issues is the creation of a stronger national government.

Task: Using information from the documents and your knowledge of United States history, write an essay in which you
• Describe the historical circumstances surrounding this constitutional or civic issue
• Explain efforts by individuals, groups, and/or governments to address this constitutional or civic issue
• Discuss the impact of the efforts on the United States and/or on American society

Guidelines: In your essay, be sure to
• Develop all aspects of the task
• Explain at least two efforts to address the issue
• Incorporate information from at least four documents
• Incorporate relevant outside information
• Support the theme with relevant facts, examples, and details
• Use a logical and clear plan of organization, including an introduction and a conclusion, that are beyond a restatement of the theme

exam_meta.part: Part III B — Civic Literacy Essay

stimulus.content: . . . In Massachusetts, during the winter of 1786, deeply indebted farmers whose land was being foreclosed refused to pay their state taxes, shut down the local courts, and seized a government arsenal. Troops from Massachusetts put down the farmers’ revolt—known as Shays’s Rebellion after its leader, Daniel Shays—while the Confederation Congress stood helpless in the crisis. “From the high ground we stood upon,” General Washington despaired in a May 18, 1786, letter to John Jay, “to be so fallen! So lost! It is really mortifying.” To national leaders, including Washington, the need for a stronger central government grew increasingly evident. Yet Americans had only recently rebelled against a tyrannical government, and remained suspicious of a concentration of government power. . . .
stimulus.image_alt: Text excerpt from Donald Ritchie describing Shays’s Rebellion of 1786 and the Confederation Congress’s helplessness during the crisis.
stimulus.citation: Source: Donald Ritchie, Our Constitution, Oxford University Press, 2006
stimulus.provenance: NYSED Regents US History & Government, June 2026, Part III

stimulus.content: An engraved illustration of fighting during Shays’ Rebellion of 1786.
stimulus.image_alt: Engraved illustration of armed men fighting during Shays’ Rebellion of 1786.
stimulus.citation: Source: New York Public Library Digital Collections (adapted)
stimulus.provenance: NYSED Regents US History & Government, June 2026, Part III

stimulus.content: Tasked with the awesome responsibility of building a Government to endure for generations to come, a band of dedicated patriots gathered in Philadelphia in 1787, seeking to build a more stable and permanent framework for a nascent [emerging] democracy. Passionate debates and intense negotiation gave way to lasting compromise, and a document emerged that became the bedrock of America. Signed on September 17, the Constitution of the United States has steered our country through ever-changing times. It guides us as leaders on the world stage and safeguards the fundamental rights of our citizens. And it guarantees that the greatness of our Nation never depends on any one person—it requires the full and active participation of an engaged and vibrant citizenry. . . .
stimulus.image_alt: Text excerpt from President Barack Obama’s 2016 Constitution Day proclamation calling the Constitution the bedrock of America.
stimulus.citation: Source: President Barack Obama, Presidential Proclamation—Constitution Day and Citizenship Day, September 16, 2016
stimulus.provenance: NYSED Regents US History & Government, June 2026, Part III

reps.exemplar:
The creation of a stronger national government was a constitutional and civic issue that turned on a core principle: how to give government enough power to function without destroying the liberty a revolution had just been fought to win. The historical circumstances made the problem impossible to ignore. Under the Articles of Confederation the national government could not tax, could not raise an effective army, and — as Document 2a shows — stood helpless in the winter of 1786 when Daniel Shays led indebted Massachusetts farmers to shut down courts and seize a government arsenal. Washington’s despair in his letter to John Jay — “to be so fallen! So lost!” — captures the moment national leaders concluded the system had failed, even as Americans “remained suspicious of a concentration of government power.”

Efforts to address the issue moved fast after Shays’ Rebellion. Delegates met at Philadelphia in 1787 and, instead of revising the Articles, wrote a new Constitution built on federalism, separation of powers, and checks and balances — outside information the documents point toward but do not supply. The ratification fight itself was an effort: Federalists argued the case in the Federalist Papers, Anti-Federalists demanded protection for individual rights, and the promise of a Bill of Rights carried the closest state conventions.

The impact has lasted longer than any of the men in these documents predicted. As Document 6 puts it, the compromise document of 1787 “became the bedrock of America,” flexible enough — through the elastic clause, the amendment process, and judicial interpretation — to steer the country through a civil war, two world wars, and a depression. The civic principle the framers proved is the one President Obama names last: the Constitution “guarantees that the greatness of our Nation never depends on any one person” — strength and limits, written into the same document.
reps.compare_focus: Name the civic principle in play — limited government made strong enough to work — and bring one piece of outside evidence the documents don’t hand you (federalism, checks and balances, the Federalist Papers, the elastic clause). The 3→4 move is outside information tied to the principle, not more document summary.
compare_checklist: Did I name the constitutional or civic principle at stake, in my own words?
Did I bring outside information — a compromise, an essay series, a constitutional clause — not found in the documents?
Did I use evidence from the documents, cited by what they are?
Did I discuss impact — what changed and what lasted — rather than only describing events?
